title: Matplotlib
description: Check that you can pick the right chart and label it so it reads on its own.

lessons.title: The pattern to learn first
lessons.lead: `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` is the form that scales to several charts in one figure.

questions.prompt: In `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`, what are `fig` and `ax`?
options: `fig` is the whole canvas; `ax` is one plotting area on it
`fig` is the chart; `ax` is the axis labels
`fig` is the x axis; `ax` is the y axis
questions.explain: You draw on the axes and save the figure. That split is what makes multi-chart figures straightforward.

options: Labels and titles being cut off at the figure edges
The order in which series are drawn
questions.explain: It recomputes the padding so nothing gets clipped. Call it after everything is drawn.

questions.prompt: Which arguments matter when saving a chart to share?
options: A filename with the format extension, such as `.png`
questions.explain: `figsize` belongs to `plt.subplots()`, when the figure is created — not to `savefig`.

lessons.title: Chart type follows the question
lessons.lead: The type you choose decides which comparison your reader can actually make.

questions.prompt: Which chart shows change over time?
questions.explain: Use a line only when the x axis has a natural order — usually time. Never for unordered categories.

questions.prompt: You want the distribution of one numeric column. Which chart?
questions.explain: A histogram bins one numeric column and counts how many records land in each bin.

questions.prompt: Which chart shows the relationship between two numeric columns?
questions.explain: Every point is one record. Scatter is how you see correlation, clusters, and outliers at once.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bar charts are true?
options: Bars must start at zero because the length is the comparison
Sort them by value unless the order carries meaning
`barh` keeps long category names readable without rotating them
A bar chart is the right choice for a time series with 200 points
questions.explain: 200 bars over time is a line chart. Bars are for comparing a manageable number of categories.

lessons.title: A chart nobody has to explain
lessons.lead: If someone sees the chart with no caption and no presenter, they should still know what it says.

questions.prompt: Which is the better chart title?
questions.explain: The title states the finding. The columns are already visible on the axes.

questions.prompt: The x tick labels overlap each other. What is the standard fix?
questions.explain: Rotating them is the quick fix; switching to `barh` is often the better one when the names are long.

questions.prompt: What belongs on a chart you are going to present?
options: Both axes labelled, with units in brackets
The source and date somewhere on the figure
An annotation on the one point that matters
A label on every data point
questions.explain: Annotating everything is the same as annotating nothing. Point at the one thing your reader should take away.

lessons.title: Everything that is not the data
lessons.lead: Chart furniture should help the reader estimate values and then get out of the way.

options: When one chart shows more than one series
Only when the chart has a grid
questions.explain: With a single series a legend is noise. With several, labelling the end of each line directly is often better still.

options: Draws the grid behind the bars instead of on top of them
Moves the x axis to the bottom of the figure
Puts the legend below the chart
questions.explain: Grid lines crossing over the data look like part of it. Push them behind.

questions.prompt: How should a grid be styled?
options: Faint — low alpha, often on one axis only
Bold, so values are easy to read off
In the same colour as the bars
questions.explain: `ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3, linestyle="--")` helps readers estimate values without competing with the data.

questions.prompt: How do you put two charts side by side in one figure?
options: `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)` then draw on `axes[0]` and `axes[1]`
Save two files and combine them afterwards
questions.explain: `subplots(rows, cols)` returns an array of axes. This is why the object-oriented form is worth learning from the start.
